title: St. Lawrence Market
brief: A piece of Toronto’s 1845 city hall is tucked inside the south market building.
note: The red-brick market that opened in 1902 incorporated the earlier city hall. Look up from the stalls to see where the civic building meets the market shed.

title: Gooderham Building
brief: Front and Wellington meet at such a sharp angle that this 1892 office building comes to a red-brick point.
note: Walk around the back toward Berczy Park. The mural on the flat west wall plays a perspective trick with the building across the street.

title: Horseshoe Tavern
brief: This Queen West room has been putting Toronto bands on stage since 1947.
note: Country acts first made the Horseshoe a destination. Its later punk and rock shows made the same small room a fixture of a different Toronto music scene.

title: Massey Hall
brief: Generations of musicians have played this 1894 hall, prized for the sound that carries from its stage to its balconies.
note: For much of the twentieth century, Massey Hall was home to the Toronto Symphony Orchestra. Its concert history also runs through jazz, folk and rock.

title: El Mocambo
brief: The Rolling Stones slipped into this Spadina club for two surprise shows in 1977.
note: The club’s neon palm tree marks a stage that has been part of Toronto’s music scene since 1948.

title: Maple Leaf Gardens
brief: Hockey once filled this entire Carlton Street building. Today an ice rink shares its shell with a grocery store.
note: The Maple Leafs moved into the Gardens in 1931. The old arena also hosted concerts, including appearances by the Beatles.

title: Art Gallery of Ontario
brief: Frank Gehry’s glass-and-timber frontage curves along Dundas Street like the hull of a ship.
note: Gehry grew up in Toronto. His expansion brought the long Galleria Italia to the street-facing side of the museum.

title: CN Tower
brief: Toronto’s skyline owes its tallest landmark to a railway company trying to improve broadcast reception.
note: Canadian National built the communications tower on former railway land. It reached its full height of just over 553 metres before opening to visitors in 1976.

title: St. James Cathedral
brief: This Gothic Revival cathedral is the fourth church to stand on its corner of King Street.
note: The parish dates to 1797. Work on the present church began in 1850 and services started in 1853.

title: Distillery District
brief: A former whisky distillery left behind a whole neighbourhood of brick factories and cobbled lanes.
note: The Gooderham and Worts works once occupied this site. Its surviving industrial buildings now house galleries, shops and restaurants.

title: Kensington Market
brief: Kensington’s market stretches through streets of houses turned into shops, rather than a single market hall.
note: Successive immigrant communities shaped the area’s street markets. The neighbourhood became a National Historic Site in 2006.

title: Sneaky Dee’s
brief: A Tex-Mex restaurant and a concert room share this corner of College and Bathurst.
note: Sneaky Dee’s opened farther north on Bloor in 1987, then moved to this intersection in 1990.

title: Lakeview Restaurant
brief: This Dundas Street diner kept late hours for workers coming off shifts at a nearby factory.
note: The Lakeview dates to 1932. Its old-fashioned diner interior later became a setting for film and television shoots.

title: Standard Theatre
brief: The corner building at Dundas and Spadina began as a Yiddish theatre and later housed the Victory Burlesque.
note: Look at the old theatre exterior from the intersection. The Victory closed in 1975; the building has since housed other businesses.

title: Barberian’s Steak House
brief: A cottage on Elm Street became a steakhouse with a two-storey wine cellar beneath it.
note: Harry Barberian opened the restaurant in 1959. The family collection inside includes paintings by members of the Group of Seven.
